messages.subject: Slow Model (Kalman Filter)
parts:
Hi all,

I started a project two months ago on Dynamic Linear Regression.
I settled on coding the Kalman Filter, which is a new topic for me.
My data has N observations for the measurement variable, Y. Each has a weight, which I've included in the noise term.
There are K regression variables.

My problem biggest problem right now, assuming I've coded the Kalman Filter properly, is that the following code runs VERY slowly.
Can anyone tell me why, or make suggestions?
I'm comfortable with y'all telling me I'm crazy stupid.

    data{

      int<lower=0> N;
      int<lower=0> K;
      vector[N] logAUR;
      vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] weight;
      matrix[N,K] Ft;
      vector[K] beta_0;
      cov_matrix[K] beta_cov0;

        }

    parameters{

      real<lower=0,upper=1> delta;
      vector[K] beta_new;
      vector<lower=0>[N] v;
      real<lower=0,upper=100> al;
      real<lower=0,upper=100> be;

        }

    transformed parameters{

      cov_matrix[K] R;
      cov_matrix[N] Q;
      vector[N] linpred;
      matrix[K,N] A;
      vector[N] err;
      vector[K] beta_mu_new;
      cov_matrix[K] beta_cov_new;

      R = beta_cov0/delta;
      linpred = Ft*beta_0;
      Q = quad_form_sym(R,Ft' )+diag_matrix(v)*diag_matrix(weight);
      A = R * Ft' * inverse(Q);
      err = logAUR-linpred;

      beta_mu_new = beta_0 + A * err;
      beta_cov_new = R - quad_form_sym(Q,A' );

        }

    model{

      al ~ uniform(0,100);
      be ~ uniform(0,100);
      delta ~ beta(al,be);

      v ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

      beta_new ~ multi_normal_cholesky(beta_mu_new,cholesky_decompose(beta_cov_new));

    }

Thanks!
Steve-0

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow Model (Kalman Filter)
parts:
Your matrix functions are very inefficient. It's
much more efficient if you can parameterize with
Cholesky factors rather than full covariance matrices.

And whatever you do, don't use diag_matrix() --- there
should be a big warning sign on that in the manual because
it fills a matrix with zeroes then proceeds to add them,
leading to a lot of unnecessary overhead. You would want
to reduce the diagonals themselves rather than creating
diagonal matrices and multiplying, and then just add that
to the diagonal of a matrix in a loop. By the time you
get all the way to multi_normal, you don't need to Cholesky
decompose because that'll be what the basic multi_normal
does internally anyway. Better if you can stick to Cholesky
factors all the way. But it's hard if you want to fiddle with
things or build a GP.

- Bob

On Tue, Dec 6, 2016 at 10:35 AM, Steve Kunec <sak...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thanks, Daniel, for the reply.
I was kind of nervous posting, as some message boards can get nasty.
We try very hard to keep that behavior off this list.

To be honest, I'm unsure if it does converge. I'm running a single chain, with a small number of iterations just to get some sort of output. It hasn't finished for many hours.
My guess was it had something to do with the matrix algebra.

N ~ 19000
K = 8

Do you have a way to simulate fake data? If so, I'd start with a smaller data set. Have you gotten a simpler model to fit? Hopefully your first Stan program isn't a full blown Kalman filter. We always suggest building up for multiple reasons: sanity, separating out computational issues from statistical issues, and it's just a lot easier to reason about it.

When Stan is "slow," it's usually not a computational issue. (Sometimes it is, but most times people post here, it's not.) There are statistical reasons why things are slow. Every iteration in Stan, when you leave the defaults, is not executed in the same amount of time. There isn't a fixed number of function evaluations that happens. NUTS allows that to vary iteration to iteration. During warmup, it's every worse because Stan is trying to find values of tuning parameters that work. If those aren't set properly, then it may take a while to finish.

The nice thing about Stan is that there are warnings that something is wrong. Your model taking a long time in warmup: you'll need to investigate. Stan's a programming language and there are lots of ways to implement something. And... there are many more ways to implement that thing incorrectly.

In short, my suggestion would be, think about the data generating process, generate a smaller data set that you can reason about, make sure your Stan program works on that. Then scale up.
I will see what happens before I repost...
You can ignore my request to see whether it's converged. When you said "slow," I had assumed you meant that it finished. If it hasn't, then I'd just start simpler.

Thanks, again!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Slow Model (Kalman Filter)
parts:
> On Dec 6, 2016, at 4:18 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Never run single chain. You can run 4 chains on your laptop for free.

With some caveats. First, you need four physical CPUs --- a lot of
people will only have two these days on a notebook. And you need
enough memory, though that's usually not a problem.

Also, it does use the four CPUs, which means they're not available
for other tasks, which can be problematic if the job's going to
run for some time. And on some machines, even running two
number crunching processes full bore will cause enough memory or
disk contention to make everything else sluggish.

So basically, your performance is going to vary with hardware.
Having said that, investing in a decent i7 4-core machine is
easily justified if you do a lot of number crunching and can
afford it.

This is one of the reasons we need a Stan-in-the-cloud solution
for people!

- Bob
